query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding 1–2 atomic percent aluminum to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance by promoting the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent Al₂O₃ scale during high-temperature exposure, without degrading its beneficial mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but exhibiting inadequate oxygen resistance (pesting) in air.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition of 1–2 at.% Al into the equiatomic composition.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 hours under low-strain or tensile loading conditions (strain rates of 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹) that preserve the original mechanical test regime.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective, continuous alumina (Al₂O₃) scale on the alloy’s surface.
generation.mechanism: At high temperature, the small amount of Al preferentially oxidizes to form Al₂O₃, a thermodynamically stable and slow-growing oxide that acts as an effective oxygen diffusion barrier. This barrier prevents further oxygen ingress into the alloy and suppresses pesting, while the low concentration is chosen to minimize any negative impact on room-temperature ductility and high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-modified alloy will exhibit substantially reduced oxidation (e.g., lower weight gain and fewer oxide-induced surface degradations) relative to the untreated material while retaining its mechanical performance at both room temperature and 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr degrades via pesting under similar conditions, showing significant oxidation without the formation of a protective oxide scale.
generation.boundary: Applicable for high-temperature applications in air at around 800 °C for durations of approximately 5 hours and under mechanical loading conditions corresponding to strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Al concentration and its precise effects on the balance of oxidation protection versus potential slight alterations in mechanical properties remain to be fully determined. There is also some uncertainty regarding the interaction of the Al₂O₃ scale with other oxide species that may form in the complex multi-element matrix.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, and (2) equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with an addition of 1–2 at.% Al. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours under controlled, low-strain tensile loading conditions (strain rates within 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹).
measurements: Weight gain measurements to quantify oxidation
Surface and cross-sectional analysis via SEM/TEM to assess the formation and continuity of the oxide scale
Post-exposure tensile tests to evaluate retention of room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped samples do not form a continuous, adherent Al₂O₃ scale (as evidenced by similar weight gain and oxide morphology to the untreated alloy) or if the modified alloy exhibits a significant degradation in mechanical properties compared to the untreated baseline, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The high temperature oxidation resistance of alloys requires alloying additions that enable the formation of an external continuous layer of a stable oxide that separates the alloy from the oxidising (corrosive) environment. This is often referred to as selective oxidation and requires that the oxide of the added element be the most stable oxide of any of the other major components in the alloy. Wagner’s theory [] indicates that for the transition from internal to external oxidation of Nb-Al alloys, alloying additions must be chosen that decrease the oxygen solubility and diffusivity and increase the diffusivity of Al in the alloy. Solutes like Hf and Cr respectively, with more negative enthalpies of formation of their oxides and smaller atomic radii than Nb, may decrease the diffusivity of oxygen by providing attractive traps [,]. Chromium, as one of the elements that increase the electron concentration in Nb, may also decrease the oxygen solubility by increasing the activity of oxygen []. Hafnium may also decrease the oxygen solubility through the gettering effect.

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. frame.system: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy in its as‐cast state, which shows 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and high yield strength (~163–530 MPa at 1000 °C) under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
frame.goal: Improve the alloy’s oxygen (oxidation) resistance at high temperatures for practical applications while preserving its beneficial mechanical properties.
frame.limitation: The alloy’s inadequate oxygen resistance, evidenced by pesting and surface degradation during high-temperature exposure in air, limits its applications despite good mechanical performance.
root_cause_cues: related studies on other refractory alloys
constraints: Preservation of room- and high-temperature mechanical performance
Utilization of a single intervention (i.e. a minimal compositional or processing change)
Exposure in air over extended durations (e.g. 5 h)
Operational strain rates consistent with those used for mechanical testing (10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹)
frame.regime: High-temperature service conditions in air between approximately 800 °C and 1000 °C under mechanical loading conditions comparable to those in tensile tests.
prior_attempts: Earlier oxidation-protection work on a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy successfully prevented pesting during a 5 h air exposure at 800 °C, likely via reactive element addition or surface modification.
Other refractory alloy studies that, while indicative of some protective mechanisms, did not specifically evaluate or achieve oxidation resistance in the equiatomic composition.
frame.understanding: A plausible hypothesis is that a minor alloying addition—such as incorporating 1–2 atomic percent aluminum—could promote the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent Al₂O₃ (alumina) scale during high-temperature exposure. This scale is known to be a highly effective oxygen diffusion barrier, thereby mitigating oxidation (pesting) without degrading the intrinsic mechanical properties of the alloy. The modified alloy is predicted to exhibit significantly reduced oxidation (lower weight gain or scaled degradation) during a controlled test at 800 °C for 5 hours in air when compared with the untreated equiatomic material. To falsify the hypothesis, a controlled experiment would involve fabricating equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with and without the 1–2 at.% Al addition, subjecting both to aging in air at 800 °C for 5 hours under a standardized low strain condition, and demonstrating that the Al-doped alloy does not form a protective alumina scale or fails to show substantial improvement in oxidation resistance relative to the baseline alloy.
